editor.capcut-desktop.notes.1.t: CapCut’s pages state neither a size limit nor 1D support – the 33-point 3D cube is the safe file.

editor.capcut-desktop.steps.0.t: Select the clip in the timeline.

editor.capcut-desktop.steps.3.t: Apply it to the clip and keep “Intensity” at 100% for a technical log conversion.

editor.capcut-mobile.notes.0.t: CapCut’s own pages describe LUT import on desktop and web only; third-party guides say the mobile app cannot import custom LUTs.

editor.capcut-mobile.steps.0.t: CapCut mobile has no known .cube import – import the LUT in CapCut desktop (Adjustment > LUT > Import) instead.

editor.capcut-mobile.steps.1.t: Or bake the conversion into the clip first (see FFmpeg), then bring the clip to mobile.

editor.davinci-resolve.notes.1.t: Use “Open LUT Folder” rather than a typed path: the folder differs by install (sources disagree on Linux; the Mac App Store build keeps its own).

editor.davinci-resolve.notes.2.t: Resolve also reads the shaper cube (1D shaper + 3D lattice in one file, Blackmagic’s layout) – a shaped 33³ beats a plain 65³ on log footage. Other editors don’t: ffmpeg rejects it, OBS reads only its 1D part.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.0.t: Open Project Settings (gear icon, bottom right) > Color Management > Lookup Tables.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.1.t: Click “Open LUT Folder” and copy the .cube into it – a subfolder becomes a submenu.

editor.davinci-resolve.steps.3.t: On the Color page, right-click a node > LUT > your LUT, or drag it from the LUTs browser onto a node.

editor.ffmpeg.notes.0.t: lut3d reads 3D cubes only (a 1D file fails with “3D LUT is empty”), sizes 2–256.

editor.ffmpeg.notes.1.t: Never hand lut3d a shaper cube – it is Resolve’s format.

editor.ffmpeg.steps.1.t: Windows drive-letter path: escape the colon inside single quotes – lut3d=file='C\:/LUTs/x.cube' – or cd into the LUT folder and use the bare file name.

editor.final-cut-pro.notes.1.t: Apple documents 3D LUT import as .cube and .mga, with no size limit stated.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.0.t: Select the clip, open the Effects browser > Color, and double-click “Custom LUT”.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.1.t: In the Video inspector’s Custom LUT section, open the LUT pop-up > “Choose Custom LUT…”, select the .cube, click Open.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.2.t: Set the Input and Output pop-ups to the color spaces the LUT converts from and to.

editor.final-cut-pro.steps.3.t: For log clips, alternatively: Info inspector > Camera LUT > “Add Custom Camera LUT…”.

editor.lumafusion.notes.1.t: Luma Touch documents .cube import “up to 64 points”, so LumaFusion gets the 33-point cube.

editor.lumafusion.steps.0.t: Copy the .cube to Files, or another location the app can reach.

editor.lumafusion.steps.1.t: Tap Import in the Library or the Color & Effects editor, choose the LUT, tap Open.

editor.lumafusion.steps.2.t: Double-tap the clip > Color & Effects > LUTs > User LUTs, and tap your LUT; keep the mix at full for a technical conversion.

editor.obs-studio.notes.0.t: “Settings only apply to SDR video” – OBS skips the filter on HDR sources.

editor.obs-studio.steps.1.t: Under “Effect Filters”, click “+” > “Apply LUT”, name it, OK.

editor.premiere-pro.notes.1.t: Premiere 25’s color management can already interpret log footage – check Lumetri Color > Settings so the log isn’t converted twice.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.0.t: Window > Lumetri Color, then select the clip in the Timeline.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.1.t: Basic Correction > “Input LUT” > “Browse…” and choose the .cube – a conversion belongs here, not under Creative > Look.

editor.premiere-pro.steps.2.t: Premiere 24 and later also offer Input LUT under Lumetri Color > Settings > Source Clip.

editor.soft.t: Menu names may vary by version.

editor.vn.notes.1.t: VN’s pages state neither a size limit nor 1D support – the 33-point 3D cube is the safe file.

editor.vn.steps.0.t: Copy the .cube to the device (e.g. the Files app).

editor.vn.steps.1.t: Select the clip > Filter > Add, choose the .cube, then a category or folder.

editor.vn.steps.2.t: Or from the Filter library: My Filters > Import Filter.

editor.vn.steps.3.t: Apply it from the category you chose in the Filter panel.

era.1860.tip.t: Before the standard observer: Maxwell’s and Helmholtz’s color triangles, three-color printing, the Munsell and Ostwald atlases.

era.1931.tip.t: CIE 1931 turns color into measurement – XYZ – followed by the first Lab spaces and NTSC color television.

era.1960.tip.t: Uniform color scales from the CIE and the OSA, Itten’s painter’s wheel, and the color signals of PAL and SECAM.

era.1976.tip.t: CIELAB and CIELUV make color distance perceptual, HSL and HSV put hue on screen, digital video gets YCbCr.

era.1990.tip.t: Rec. 709 and sRGB set the screen standard, Adobe RGB and ProPhoto widen it for photography, Cineon scans film.

era.2000.tip.t: CIECAM02 unifies color appearance, DCI-P3 defines digital cinema, camera makers ship their first log curves.

era.2010.tip.t: HDR and wide gamut – Rec. 2020, PQ, HLG – plus ACES for cinema, CAM16, and a log curve from every camera maker.

era.2020.tip.t: OKLab and OKLCH reach CSS, Material Design adopts HCT, log recording comes to phones.

faq.css.p1.t: Natively rgb(), hsl(), hwb(), lab(), lch(), oklab(), oklch(), plus color() for Display P3, Adobe RGB, ProPhoto, linear sRGB and XYZ (D65 and D50). CSS's rec2020 is a pure 2.4 gamma, not the BT.2020 curve of this catalog's Rec. 2020 – the same numbers would name a different color. Each dossier's css tab writes the current color in copyable form; spaces CSS lacks ship as ICC profiles or LUTs instead.

faq.css.q.t: Which of these can CSS write?

faq.cvd.p1.t: Open View and pick a Vision: red-blind (protanopia), green-blind (deuteranopia) or blue-blind (tritanopia). The catalog redraws as that eye sees it, so you can check that the colors of a palette stay apart. About 1 in 12 men have a color vision deficiency, by the NEI's count.

faq.cvd.q.t: How do colors look to color-blind people?

faq.exact.p1.t: Conversions are closed formulas, not lookup approximations, and round trips return within floating-point noise. The few exceptions are documented where they occur: OSA-UCS has no closed inverse, atlas systems like Munsell interpolate between published grades, and rgb output is never clamped: a color outside sRGB comes back below 0 or past 255, so clamp only when you display it.

faq.exact.p2.t: They are also checked: every space links the paper or spec it implements, values are tested against colorjs.io wherever the two overlap, and the camera logs against the Academy's official ACES transforms. formula-verification.md records what was checked against what – including a few places where the published papers themselves had errors.

faq.exact.p3.t: If the numbers differ from another library's, compare ranges: this one keeps each space's conventional ranges – RGB 0–255, Lab lightness 0–100, hue 0–360 – where many flatten everything to 0–1. Every card shows its ranges; in code they're space.oklch.range.

faq.exact.q.t: Are conversions exact? Do round trips lose data?

faq.gamut.p1.t: A color one space can describe but another – or your screen – can't show. A vivid Display P3 green doesn't exist in sRGB: convert it, and the numbers fall outside the valid range. The atlas keeps this visible: the pill next to the current color names the tightest standard gamut that holds it, and out-of-range stretches ghost over a checkerboard.

faq.hex.p1.t: Type or paste it into the color field at the top, say #ff8000. Every space on the page shows that color at once; in OKLCH it reads 0.732, 0.186, 53, which CSS writes as oklch(0.732 0.186 53). Each dossier's css tab gives the copyable form, and in code it's space.rgb.oklch(255, 128, 0).

faq.hex.q.t: How do I convert hex to OKLCH?

faq.hsl.p1.t: OKLCH. It keeps the same three controls – hue, chroma, lightness – but its lightness is trustworthy: in HSL, yellow at L=50 emits about 13 times the light of blue at L=50, so equal L doesn't mean equal brightness. In OKLCH it does. CSS supports oklch() natively.

faq.hsl.q.t: What should I use instead of HSL?

faq.log.p1.t: Open your camera's log space, such as S-Log3, LogC4 or Apple Log. In its conversion LUT block, choose Rec. 709 and your editor: DaVinci Resolve, Premiere Pro, Final Cut Pro, OBS, ffmpeg and others. Your browser writes the .cube file. It is a technical conversion with no tone mapping: highlights above diffuse white clip, and the look is yours to add.

faq.log.q.t: How do I convert S-Log3 or another camera log to Rec. 709?

faq.model.p1.t: A color model is a shape for the numbers: RGB says three primaries, HSL says hue, saturation and lightness, CMYK says four inks. A color space ties a model to measurable light – which primaries, which white, which curve – so each set of numbers names exactly one color. rgb(255 0 0) is a different red in sRGB, Display P3 and Adobe RGB: one model, three spaces.

faq.model.p2.t: Everyday usage calls both spaces – so does CSS's color-mix(in hsl, …), and so does this catalog. A model without an anchor of its own borrows one: HSL and HSV here reshape sRGB, as in CSS.

faq.model.q.t: Color model or color space – what's the difference?

faq.muddy.p1.t: Because they're computed in gamma-encoded sRGB, where averaging two colors' numbers produces darker, duller light than actually mixing their light would. Interpolating in OKLab avoids this; in CSS that's linear-gradient(in oklab, red, blue). Every dossier's interpolate row draws the same blend through two spaces side by side, so you can see the difference before choosing.

faq.muddy.q.t: Why do my gradients turn muddy in the middle?

faq.pantone.p1.t: Those are licensed products: their colors are defined by data the owners sell, not by published formulas – so there's no open math to implement, and redistributing their tables wouldn't be legal. Close relatives whose math is public are here: Munsell (its 1943 renotation is public record) and RAL Design (defined directly in CIELAB). Any system whose math was ever published belongs here; suggest one that's missing.

faq.photo.p1.t: For the web and for sharing, sRGB: browsers and phones assume it when a file carries no profile. Display P3 keeps more of a vivid scene on Apple and many Android screens, as long as the profile stays embedded. Send Adobe RGB when a print lab asks for it. Keep ProPhoto RGB for 16-bit editing: its gamut is so wide that 8-bit files band.

faq.photo.q.t: Which color space should I export photos in?

faq.print.p1.t: A screen emits light; paper reflects what its inks don't absorb. Ink on paper reaches fewer vivid colors – saturated RGB blues, greens and reds fall outside it – so they print duller. Prepress converts through an ICC profile made for the press and paper, such as FOGRA39 for European coated stock or GRACoL in the US. This catalog's CMYK is the plain formula CSS uses for device-cmyk() without a profile – right for the numbers, not a proof of the print.

faq.print.q.t: Why does print look duller than the screen?

faq.what.p1.t: A coordinate system for color: axes, ranges, and a rule tying the numbers to measurable light. Human vision is trichromatic — the retina has three types of cone cells (S, M, L) — so three coordinates are the minimum needed to describe any color a human eye can perceive. The same orange is rgb(255 128 0), oklch(0.732 0.186 53) and XYZ [49, 36.7, 4.5]. A palette is a handful of chosen colors; a space is a way to write down any color at all.

faq.which.li1.t: storing and sharing images – sRGB, the web's default;

faq.which.li2.t: designing palettes and gradients – OKLCH, where equal steps look equal;

faq.which.li3.t: math on light (blending, blurring, 3D) – linear-light RGB;

faq.which.li4.t: shooting and grading video – your camera's log space, delivered in Rec. 709 or Rec. 2100;

faq.which.li5.t: measuring how different two colors look – CIELAB or DIN99o.

faq.which.p2.t: To see every space sorted by task, group the catalog by purpose.

faq.which.q.t: Which space should I actually use?

lore.a98rgb.for.t: a Photoshop working space reaching printable cyans and greens

lore.a98rgb.sin.t: born of a bug – an engineer transcribed SMPTE 240M primaries wrong, and the accident shipped

lore.aces2065-1.for.t: the archival master – AP0 primaries wrap everything visible

lore.aces2065-1.nm.t: named for its SMPTE standard number, ST 2065-1

lore.aces2065-1.sin.t: AP0 is mostly imaginary: great vault, terrible working space

lore.acescc.for.t: pure-log grading space – dials feel like film printer lights

lore.acescc.sin.t: pure log has no toe: near-black codes get twitchy

lore.acescct.for.t: ACEScc with a toe, so lifted blacks grade like film

lore.acescct.nm.t: the extra t is the toe

lore.acescg.for.t: the render/compositing space of the ACES pipeline – linear, wide but real

lore.acescg.nm.t: CG = computer graphics; primaries called AP1

lore.acesproxy.for.t: on-set monitoring log – integer-friendly, never stored

lore.anlab.for.t: chromatic-valence ΔE for textiles – the direct ancestor of CIELAB

lore.apple-rgb.for.t: the classic Mac Trinitron display, frozen as a profile

lore.applelog.for.t: ProRes Log on iPhone 15 Pro – a phone speaking cinema

lore.applelog2.for.t: Apple Log off the BT.2020 container – the same curve on primaries tuned to iPhone sensors

lore.atd95.for.t: the opponent pathway itself – discrimination and adaptation, not just appearance

lore.awg3.for.t: one fixed camera RGB for ALEXA footage, so VFX can invert Log C to scene linear and convert with a single matrix

lore.awg3.nm.t: formerly ALEXA Wide Gamut RGB; 3 = ARRI’s third color-science generation

lore.awg4.for.t: the ALEXA 35’s gamut, defined within ACES AP0 alongside LogC4

lore.awg4.sin.t: CAT02-adapted into an ACES AP0 container, its outer edge can still go negative (ARRI’s own spec warns of it)

lore.bestrgb.for.t: Don RGB 4 widened to hold Fujichrome Velvia’s saturated reds and magentas

lore.bestrgb.sin.t: its blue lies just outside the spectral locus – about 3.5% of code values encode no real color

lore.betargb.for.t: the smallest RGB gamut that holds a reference set of film, chart and printing colors

lore.betargb.sin.t: 10- and 12-ink pigment inkjets exceed it in the cyans and blues – the reason Russell RGB exists

lore.bmdwg.for.t: the camera gamut of Blackmagic’s Gen 5 color science, decoded from Blackmagic RAW

lore.bmdwg.nm.t: BMD = Blackmagic Design; Gen 5 = its fifth color-science generation

lore.bmdwg.sin.t: its white is published as D65 to seven digits (0.3127170, 0.3290312), so tools that keep it and tools that use 4-digit D65 disagree by up to ~2.5e-4

lore.brucergb.for.t: a safe 8-bit editing space between ColorMatch RGB’s cyan clipping and Adobe RGB (1998)’s unprintable excess

lore.brucergb.nm.t: named after its author, Bruce Fraser

lore.brucergb.sin.t: clips fully saturated yellows about as much as Adobe RGB (1998)

lore.cam02-ucs.for.t: CIECAM02 as a uniform space – the ΔE workhorse of the 2010s

lore.cam16-lcd.for.t: the variant tuned for large differences

lore.cam16-scd.for.t: the variant tuned for small differences

lore.cam16-ucs.for.t: CAM16 squeezed into a uniform space – modern ΔE work

lore.cam16.for.t: fix CIECAM02’s numerical failures with one cleaner adaptation transform

lore.cam16.nm.t: CAM = colour appearance model; 16 is 2016, the year CIE adopted it

lore.cam16.sin.t: a full viewing-conditions model: powerful, and overkill anywhere conditions are unknown

lore.cct-duv.for.t: specifying white light with both warm–cool temperature and green–pink tint

lore.cct-duv.nm.t: correlated color temperature plus signed distance in CIE 1960 uv

lore.cct-duv.sin.t: meaningful only near the Planckian locus; it discards luminance

lore.cie-rgb.for.t: the primaries of the Wright–Guild experiments that defined the standard observer

lore.cie-rgb.sin.t: needs negative red to match spectral cyans – the very problem XYZ was invented to hide

lore.ciecam02.for.t: the committee appearance model behind Windows Color System

lore.ciecam02.nm.t: CAM = colour appearance model; 02 is the year, 2002

lore.ciecam02.sin.t: its CAT02 matrix can go negative for saturated blues – the defect that begat CAM16

lore.cineon.for.t: film scans as printing density – the grandfather of every camera log

lore.clog.nm.t: C is Canon – a different “C” from ARRI’s Log C, where C is for Cineon

lore.clog3.for.t: the in-between: more range than C-Log, friendlier than C-Log2

lore.cmy.for.t: subtractive mixing at its simplest – the teaching model

lore.cmyk.for.t: process printing’s four plates as a space

lore.cmyk.nm.t: K is the key plate – the one others register to – not “blacK”

lore.cmyk.sin.t: the naive formula: real separation needs ICC profiles, ink limits and black generation

lore.colormatch.for.t: matching Radius PressView calibrated monitors in professional graphic arts

lore.colormatch.sin.t: clips printable cyans and the blues and greens next to them (Fraser, 2000)

lore.coloroid.for.t: aesthetic spacing for architects – harmony intervals, not ΔE

lore.coloroid.nm.t: A·T·V: árnyalat, telítettség, világosság – hue, saturation, lightness in Hungarian

lore.davinci.for.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut Intermediate – one grading space for any camera

lore.davinci.nm.t: named for DaVinci Resolve, Blackmagic’s own grading software

lore.dcdm.for.t: the projector’s master format: XYZ with a 2.6 gamma

lore.dci-p3-plus.for.t: more saturated color than DCI-P3 from the Canon EOS C500, keeping the DCI white

lore.dci-p3-plus.sin.t: its blue primary has y = −0.09 – outside the visible gamut, so part of the code range is imaginary

lore.dci-p3.for.t: a gamut real xenon projectors could cover

lore.dci-p3.sin.t: its native white is greenish ~6300 K cinema white, not D65 – grading for TV needs adaptation

lore.dgamut.for.t: DJI’s cinema gamut, covering Rec.709 and DCI-P3 with primaries aligned to P3’s so hues hold in gamut mapping

lore.dgamut.sin.t: its published matrix has 4 decimals, so RGB white lands 6e-5 off D65

lore.din99.for.t: a Euclidean stand-in for CIE94: plain distance in the space tracks ΔE94, no weighting functions

lore.din99.sin.t: blue tolerance ellipses stay elongated – the defect the 2002 b/c/d revisions set out to fix

lore.din99c.for.t: DIN99 with the blue fixed: a share of Z mixed into X before CIELAB rounds the blue tolerance ellipses

lore.din99c.nm.t: “c” is sequential – the second of the 2002 revisions b, c, d

lore.din99d.for.t: the DIN99 revision tuned for small differences

lore.din99d.nm.t: “d” is sequential, after b and c – not an acronym, just the third 2002 revision

lore.din99o-lab.for.t: warp Lab so plain Euclidean distance works as ΔE

lore.din99o-lab.nm.t: “99” is the year, “o” the optimized revision

lore.dkl.for.t: the axes LGN neurons actually respond to – cone-opponent, isoluminant

lore.dlog.nm.t: D is DJI – distinct from D-Log M, the separate curve on DJI’s consumer drones

lore.donrgb4.for.t: holding the Ektachrome film gamut with virtually no clipping

lore.donrgb4.nm.t: Don Hutcheson’s fourth trial version, named in 1996 by Apple ColorSync product manager Damon Rando

lore.dsh.for.t: colorimetry’s classic triple: dominant wavelength, saturation, brightness – Helmholtz coordinates

lore.dsh.sin.t: purples have no dominant wavelength, only a complementary one – the space folds there

lore.dwg.for.t: one wide gamut DaVinci Resolve converts every camera into before grading

lore.dwg.nm.t: named for DaVinci Resolve, Blackmagic’s grading software

lore.dwg.sin.t: its whitepaper shipped wrong matrix values and a wrong green x, fixed in v1.0.1 (2020) and v1.1 (2021)

lore.ecirgb.for.t: print-oriented RGB for European prepress, encoded so equal code steps are equal L* steps

lore.ecirgb.nm.t: ECI = European Color Initiative; v2 (2007) replaced v1’s gamma 1.8 with the L* curve

lore.egamut.for.t: FilmLight’s camera-agnostic working gamut under T-Log in Baselight

lore.erimm.nm.t: ER = extended range, stretching RIMM’s headroom

lore.filmicpro.for.t: the app log that made phones gradeable

lore.flog.nm.t: F is Fujifilm; F-Gamut, its matching primaries, shares BT.2020 chromaticities

lore.flog2c.for.t: F-Log2 with room for more saturated color – the same curve, on a gamut that encloses BT.2020

lore.flog2c.nm.t: the F-Log2 curve recorded on F-Gamut C

lore.gplog2.for.t: pure-log capture on GoPro’s MISSION 1 series – log base 600, clipping about 1.8 stops above white

lore.gplog2.sin.t: GoPro’s docs quote clip-relative linear (18% grey = 0.0517); scene linear here is 2^1.8 larger – the LUT generator’s default +1.8 EV – so mixing the two shifts exposure by 1.8 stops

lore.hcg.for.t: HSV refactored as chroma plus gray base

lore.hcl.for.t: hue–chroma–luminance picker math (not the Lab-based LCh)

lore.hct.for.t: dynamic theming: pick tone for contrast, keep hue and chroma honest

lore.hct.sin.t: two models stitched together – CAM16 hue/chroma with Lab tone – so the inverse needs a solver

lore.hcy.nm.t: hue · chroma · luma – Y is Rec.601 luma, not lightness

lore.hdr-cie-lab.for.t: Lab rebuilt for HDR – the cube root swapped for a luminance-aware curve

lore.hdr-ipt.for.t: IPT rebuilt for HDR luminance ranges

lore.hellwig2022.for.t: CAM16 pruned to what vision data actually supports

lore.hellwig2022.nm.t: named for its authors, Hellwig & Fairchild, and their 2022 paper

lore.helmgen.for.t: Oklab-style gradients without the dark-end cusps or purple blue-to-white midpoints

lore.helmgen.nm.t: Helmlab’s generation space (GenSpace); its sibling MetricSpace is for ΔE

lore.helmgen.sin.t: refit between releases – v0.10’s softened cube root became v0.11’s depressed cubic – so coordinates depend on the version

lore.helmgenlch.for.t: the polar form of HelmGen, for hue-led ramps

lore.hpluv.for.t: the pastel variant – chroma capped so every hue can reach it

lore.hpluv.sin.t: only pastels: the cap is the dullest hue’s maximum

lore.hsi.for.t: machine-vision variant where I is the plain mean of R,G,B

lore.hsi.sin.t: hue is numerically unstable near gray – sensor noise sends it spinning

lore.hsl.for.t: hue controls cheap enough for 1970s framebuffers

lore.hsl.nm.t: lightness – the double-cone: L=100 is always white

lore.hsl.sin.t: L=50 is not one brightness: yellow at L=50 emits ~13× the luminance of blue

lore.hsluv.for.t: an HSL that never lies about lightness – L is CIE L*, saturation is share of the possible chroma

lore.hsm.for.t: hue–saturation–mixture, built for skin segmentation research

lore.hsp.for.t: HSV with a brightness that matches the eye

lore.hsp.nm.t: P = perceived brightness, a weighted RMS of R,G,B

lore.hsv.for.t: painter-style “tints and shades” for early paint programs

lore.hsv.nm.t: aka HSB; V=100 is the pure hue, not white

lore.hsv.sin.t: V is just max(R,G,B): full-value blue and yellow claim equal brightness and are nowhere near

lore.hunt.for.t: the whole appearance picture – rods included – from starlight to bright daylight

lore.hunt.nm.t: named for Robert Hunt, who built it over three decades at Kodak

lore.hunt.sin.t: so many viewing-condition parameters that two faithful implementations rarely agree

lore.hunter-rdab.for.t: reflectance plus opponent readings that 1940s analog colorimeters could compute from X, Y, Z

lore.hunter-rdab.sin.t: a and b shrink as Rd falls toward black; the empirical f(Y) factor only slows the collapse

lore.hwb.for.t: mixing the way painters think – a hue plus white plus black

lore.hwb.nm.t: hue · whiteness · blackness, now native in CSS

lore.hwb.sin.t: W+B>100 produces gray; hue no longer affects the result

lore.iapbp.for.t: a uniform HDR/WCG space with low lightness–chroma crosstalk for image processing

lore.iapbp.sin.t: no published inverse, code or worked example, and its reference white’s luminance is never stated

lore.icacb.for.t: an HDR ΔE space in the ICtCp family

space.a98rgb-linear.desc.t: Linear-light Adobe RGB — the gamma-free counterpart to Adobe RGB 1998, sharing its wider-than-sRGB primaries and D65 white point but with channel values directly proportional to light intensity. It is the intermediate space for accurate color math, before results are re-encoded with Adobe RGB's transfer curve.

space.a98rgb-linear.use.t: Intermediate linear-light space for Adobe RGB color math; current, used before re-encoding to Adobe RGB's gamma curve.

space.a98rgb.desc.t: Adobe RGB — introduced by Adobe in 1998 as a wider-gamut alternative to sRGB, designed to reproduce more of the cyans and greens achievable in CMYK printing. It keeps sRGB's D65 white point but uses different primaries and a slightly different gamma. It remains a standard working space in photography and print production, where sRGB's narrower gamut would clip too much color.

space.a98rgb.use.t: Wide-gamut photography and print working space; still common where sRGB's gamut clips CMYK-reproducible colors.

space.aces2065-1.desc.t: ACES2065-1 — the Academy Color Encoding System's archival and interchange master format, built on the AP0 primaries, wide enough to enclose the entire visible gamut, with ACES's characteristic white point near D60. Like ACEScg it stores scene-referred light linearly, with values reaching far past nominal white to hold highlight detail for later grading or rendering. AMPAS designed it as the long-term, camera-agnostic exchange format for finished ACES masters, distinct from ACEScg's smaller AP1 primaries used for day-to-day rendering.

space.aces2065-1.use.t: Archival/interchange master encoding for finished ACES film and TV masters; current long-term storage format (SMPTE ST 2065-1).

space.acescc.desc.t: ACEScc — the Academy Color Encoding System's logarithmic grading space, sharing the AP1 primaries with ACEScg but applying a pure log2 curve so exposure stops map to code values the way film-trained colorists expect. Unlike its sibling ACEScct, it has no linear toe near black, favoring mathematical purity over legacy grading-control behavior. It's used as the working space for color grading within ACES-managed post-production pipelines, ahead of final render back to ACEScg or ACES2065-1.

space.acescc.use.t: Log2 color-grading working space in ACES post-production; current, though largely superseded by ACEScct on legacy grading control surfaces.

space.acescct.desc.t: ACEScct — the Academy Color Encoding System's other grading space, sharing ACEScg's AP1 primaries and ACEScc's log2 curve but adding a linear toe near black. That toe keeps traditional lift/gamma/gain color-corrector controls behaving the way colorists expect instead of exaggerating noise in the shadows, which is why ACEScct is generally preferred over ACEScc on control surfaces built for legacy grading tools.

space.acescct.use.t: Log2-with-toe color-grading working space in ACES post-production; current default ACES grading space.

space.acescg.desc.t: ACEScg — the Academy Color Encoding System's linear working space, defined by AMPAS in 2014 for CGI rendering and visual-effects compositing. Built on the wide AP1 primaries, it stores scene-referred light linearly rather than through a log curve, with headroom above white for highlights and light sources that would otherwise clip. It's the standard render and composite space in VFX and animation pipelines built around ACES.

space.acescg.use.t: Linear render/composite working space for CGI and VFX; current standard in ACES-based VFX/animation pipelines.

space.acesproxy.desc.t: ACESproxy — the Academy's on-set monitoring and preview encoding, built to carry AP1 linear-light images as 10-bit legal-range code values over standard SDI video cables during production. It's a coarse, quantized encoding meant for on-set color decisions, dailies, and viewfinder-style preview — not for storage, compositing, or final grading, where ACEScc or ACEScct take over once footage reaches post.

space.acesproxy.loss-note.t: Integral SDI code values by design; decode-encode snaps to the 10-bit lattice.

space.acesproxy.use.t: On-set monitoring and dailies preview encoding over SDI video; current but narrow-purpose, not used for storage or final grading.

space.anlab.desc.t: ANLAB is the chromatic-valence opponent space developed by Adams in 1942 and extended by Nickerson in 1950 — the direct ancestor of CIELAB. It builds lightness and two opponent color channels by running each adapted tristimulus ratio through the Munsell Renotation System's empirical value function and then taking differences between the results, the same opponent-color logic CIELAB later kept while replacing that iterative Munsell function with a closed-form cube root in 1976. ANLAB saw substantial industrial use for color-difference measurement in the decades before CIELAB standardized the field.

space.anlab.successor-note.t: CIELAB kept its opponent logic and swapped the Munsell function for a cube root

space.anlab.use.t: Industrial color-difference measurement; historical, superseded by CIELAB and CIEDE2000.

space.apple-rgb.desc.t: Apple RGB — the working space used by classic Mac OS, modeling the color response of Apple's original Trinitron CRT displays. Referenced to the D65 white point with a gamma of about 1.8, Apple's historic system default, it remained a common Photoshop working space for years and is still encountered in millions of legacy image files.

space.apple-rgb.successor-note.t: sRGB became the default of Windows, the web and Photoshop 5

space.apple-rgb.use.t: Legacy Mac / Photoshop RGB working space (D65, γ 1.8) from the 13″ AppleColor monitor; obsolete, superseded by sRGB.

space.applelog.desc.t: Apple Log — Apple's log profile, introduced with the iPhone 15 Pro in 2023 for ProRes Log recording aimed at professional and cinematic video workflows, with tight integration into Final Cut Pro's color tools. Its curve opens with a quadratic toe near black before switching to a log2 highlight region, extending recordable dynamic range well beyond the phone's standard video profiles. It's defined over BT.2020 primaries, matching the wide-gamut sensors across the iPhone Pro line.

space.applelog.use.t: Cinema-oriented log capture on iPhone Pro for ProRes Log workflows; current native encoding since the iPhone 15 Pro.

space.applelog2.desc.t: Apple Log 2 — Apple's second log encoding for iPhone video, specified in Apple's September 2025 white paper. It keeps the Apple Log transfer function unchanged, a log2 curve that rolls into a parabola near black to better hold negative noise values, so 18% grey still lands at 0.4883. What changes is the gamut: instead of the BT.2020 container Apple Log records into, Apple Log 2 encodes Apple Wide Gamut, a D65 primary set Apple optimized for its camera sensors in scene-referred work.

space.applelog2.use.t: Log capture on iPhone in Apple's own wide gamut for grading and VFX; Apple's current log encoding (white paper Sept 2025).

space.atd95.desc.t: ATD95 — Sherman Lee Guth's final ATD model (1995), a vision-science account of the opponent pathways: retinal illuminance drives gain-controlled cone responses into two sequential opponent stages — A (achromatic), T (tritan, red-green) and D (deutan, yellow-blue) — modelling discrimination and adaptation data rather than appearance scales. Guth himself stressed it "cannot be considered a colour appearance model"; it ships here as the coordinate system of its second (large-field) stage, the one his hue and saturation predictions read from.

space.atd95.use.t: Historical vision-science opponent model (discrimination, not appearance); kept for study.

space.awg3.desc.t: ARRI Wide Gamut 3 – the camera RGB primaries of ARRI's third color-science generation, published by ARRI in 2011 as ALEXA Wide Gamut RGB and renamed ARRI Wide Gamut 3 in the LogC4 specification. The primaries are virtual, placed to hold the colors the ALEXA sensor records rather than to match any display. This is the scene-linear form: decoded LogC3 data, scaled so a white diffusing reflector reads 1.0, with highlights above it. It is the gamut of the ALEXA Classic, XT, SXT, Mini, LF, Mini LF and 65 and the AMIRA.

space.awg3.successor-note.t: ARRI's fourth color-science generation, with the ALEXA 35, moved to ARRI Wide Gamut 4

space.awg3.use.t: Scene-linear camera gamut beneath LogC3 for ALEXA/AMIRA footage in VFX and grading; still active, succeeded by AWG4 on the ALEXA 35.

space.awg4.desc.t: ARRI Wide Gamut 4 – the RGB primaries of ARRI's fourth color-science generation, introduced with the ALEXA 35 in 2022 and paired with the LogC4 curve. Its red primary is ACES AP0's red and its green sits on AP0's red-green edge, so the gamut lies within AP0. This is the scene-linear form: decoded LogC4 data before any display transform, with highlights above 1.0.

space.awg4.use.t: Scene-linear camera gamut beneath LogC4 for ALEXA 35 footage in VFX and grading; current ARRI standard.

space.bestrgb.desc.t: Best RGB – Don Hutcheson's variant of Don RGB 4 with the red primary moved onto the spectral locus at 700 nm, to enclose the saturated reds and magentas of Fujichrome Velvia film, and a slightly more saturated green. Its blue, shared with Don RGB 4, lies just outside the locus, so about 3.5% of its code values encode no real color. Like Don RGB 4 it uses a D50 white and gamma 2.2 and is distributed as an ICC profile.

space.bestrgb.use.t: Wide-gamut photo working space for saturated film scans; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.betargb.desc.t: Beta RGB – a working space Bruce Lindbloom derived as the smallest RGB gamut that encloses a reference set of film, color-chart and printing colors, so it holds them with less wasted code range than larger spaces such as ProPhoto RGB. Its white is D50, the white of ICC profiles and Photoshop's Lab, chosen to avoid an adaptation step, and it uses gamma 2.2: Lindbloom's own perturbation analysis found an optimum near 2.12 and he kept the conventional value.

space.betargb.use.t: Optimized capture, archiving and editing working space for high-end photo work; niche.

space.bmdfilm.desc.t: Blackmagic Film — Blackmagic Design's log curve for its Generation 5 color science, which debuted on the URSA Mini Pro 12K and rolled out across the Pocket Cinema Camera line. It combines a linear toe near black with a natural-log highlight region to hold detail across the sensor's full dynamic range for grading in DaVinci Resolve. It pairs with the BMD Wide Gamut Gen5 primaries and ships inside Blackmagic RAW (BRAW) footage.

space.bmdfilm.use.t: Log curve for Blackmagic cinema cameras shooting BRAW; current on URSA Mini Pro/Pocket Cinema Gen 5 color-science bodies.

space.bmdwg.desc.t: Blackmagic Wide Gamut (Gen 5) – the camera RGB primaries of Blackmagic Design's Generation 5 color science, introduced in 2020 and paired with the Blackmagic Film Gen 5 log curve in Blackmagic RAW. All three of its primaries are virtual, outside the spectral locus, placed to hold what the sensor records. This is the scene-linear form, before the log curve, with highlights above 1.0.

space.bmdwg.use.t: Scene-linear camera gamut beneath Blackmagic Film Gen 5 for BRAW footage in VFX and grading; current on Gen 5 color-science cameras.

space.brucergb.desc.t: Bruce RGB – a working space Bruce Fraser published in 1998 as a safe, output-oriented choice for Photoshop 5 users editing 8-bit images heavily. He designed it as a compromise between ColorMatch RGB, which clips printable cyans, and Adobe RGB (1998), which spends code values on colors few printers reach. It shares the red and blue primaries and D65 white of sRGB and Adobe RGB (1998), differs only in its green, and uses gamma 2.2.

space.brucergb.use.t: Conservative-gamut RGB working space for heavily edited 8-bit images; legacy.

space.cam02-lcd.desc.t: CAM02-LCD is a variant of the CAM02-UCS uniform color space that Luo, Cui & Li tuned in 2006 specifically for LARGE color differences, rather than the small, fine-grained differences most difference formulas target. Like CAM02-UCS, it reprojects CIECAM02's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean, Cartesian layout, but with scaling calibrated against large-difference visual data. CAM16-LCD later carried the same large-difference calibration over to CAM16.

space.cam02-lcd.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-lcd.use.t: Uniform space for large color-difference/gamut-mapping work; largely superseded by CAM16-LCD.

space.cam02-scd.desc.t: CAM02-SCD is a variant of the CAM02-UCS uniform color space that Luo, Cui & Li tuned in 2006 specifically for SMALL color differences, such as those relevant to tolerance and quality-control judgments. Like CAM02-UCS, it reprojects CIECAM02's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean, Cartesian layout, but with scaling calibrated against small, near-threshold visual differences. CAM16-SCD later carried the same small-difference calibration over to CAM16.

space.cam02-scd.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-scd.use.t: Uniform space for small color-difference tolerance/QC judgments; largely superseded by CAM16-SCD.

space.cam02-ucs.desc.t: CAM02-UCS is the uniform color space Luo, Cui & Li built on top of CIECAM02 in 2006, transforming its lightness and colorfulness correlates through a compressive scale so that equal numerical distances correspond much more closely to equal perceived color differences. Reprojected into Cartesian coordinates, it behaves like a CIELAB-style space but is far more perceptually uniform, so it is well suited to computing color differences (ΔE) and to gamut mapping. CAM16-UCS later carried the same compression scheme over to CAM16.

space.cam02-ucs.successor-note.t: Rebuilt on CAM16 when CAM16 replaced CIECAM02

space.cam02-ucs.use.t: General-purpose uniform space for delta-E computation and gamut mapping; superseded by CAM16-UCS but still in wide use – matplotlib's viridis was designed in it.

space.cam16-lcd.desc.t: CAM16-LCD is a variant of the CAM16-UCS uniform color space that Li et al. tuned in 2017 specifically for LARGE color differences, carrying over compression coefficients from Luo, Cui & Li's 2006 work on perceptually uniform CIECAM spaces. Like CAM16-UCS it reprojects CAM16's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean, Cartesian layout, but its scaling is calibrated against large-difference visual data rather than the small, fine-grained differences most color-difference formulas target — the CAM16 counterpart to CAM02-LCD.

space.cam16-lcd.use.t: Uniform space for large color-difference/gamut-mapping comparisons; current default for that role.

space.cam16-scd.desc.t: CAM16-SCD is a variant of the CAM16-UCS uniform color space that Li et al. tuned in 2017 specifically for SMALL color differences, carrying over compression coefficients from Luo, Cui & Li's 2006 work on perceptually uniform CIECAM spaces. Like CAM16-UCS it reprojects CAM16's lightness and colorfulness into a near-Euclidean, Cartesian layout, but its scaling is calibrated against small, near-threshold visual differences rather than the coarser comparisons CAM16-LCD targets — the CAM16 counterpart to CAM02-SCD.

space.cam16-scd.use.t: Uniform space for small color-difference tolerance/QC comparisons; current default for that role.

space.cam16-ucs.desc.t: CAM16-UCS is the uniform color space Li et al. built on top of CAM16 in their 2017 paper, transforming CAM16's lightness and colorfulness correlates through a compressive scale so that equal numerical distances correspond much more closely to equal perceived color differences. Reprojected into Cartesian coordinates, it behaves like a CIELAB-style space but is far more perceptually uniform, so it is well suited to computing color differences (ΔE) and to gamut mapping, where straight-line distance needs to track actual visual difference.

space.cam16-ucs.use.t: General-purpose uniform space for delta-E computation and gamut mapping; current default successor to CAM02-UCS.

space.cam16.desc.t: CAM16 is the color appearance model introduced by Li et al. in 2017 as a simplified, more robust successor to CIECAM02. It predicts how a color actually looks to a human observer under specific viewing conditions — accounting for the surrounding light, background, and the eye's state of adaptation — rather than merely describing the raw stimulus, yielding correlates of lightness, colorfulness, and hue (plus chroma, saturation, and brightness in the full model). Google adopted it, via its HCT derivative, as the foundation of Material Design's dynamic color system, and it is now the default replacement for CIECAM02 across color science.

space.cam16.use.t: Color-appearance modeling of perceived lightness/colorfulness/hue; current default replacement for CIECAM02, basis of Material Design's HCT.

space.cct-duv.desc.t: CCT + Duv — the lighting industry's two-coordinate description of near-white chromaticity. Correlated colour temperature locates the nearest point on the Planckian locus; Duv is the signed perpendicular distance from that locus in the CIE 1960 uv diagram (positive above the locus, conventionally greener; negative below it, conventionally pinker). Unlike CCT alone, the pair preserves both dimensions of chromaticity around the white-light region.

space.cct-duv.loss-note.t: Chromaticity only: luminance is discarded; the inverse reconstructs XYZ at Y=100.

space.cct-duv.use.t: Lighting specification and LED binning: CCT says warm–cool, Duv says green–pink; current companion coordinates for white-light chromaticity.

space.cie-rgb.desc.t: CIE RGB — the experimental color space built directly from the 1931 Wright-Guild color-matching experiments, whose data became the foundation for the CIE XYZ standard itself. Its three primaries are monochromatic single-wavelength lights rather than the broadband primaries of any real display, referenced to an equal-energy white point. It survives today mainly as a historical and pedagogical space — the common ancestor from which nearly every later RGB space descends.

space.cie-rgb.successor-note.t: Its color-matching functions go negative, so the CIE adopted all-positive XYZ the same year

space.cie-rgb.use.t: Historical/pedagogical reference space built from the Wright-Guild matching data; obsolete in production, ancestor of CIE XYZ.

space.ciecam02.desc.t: CIECAM02 is the color appearance model published by the CIE in 2002, developed to predict how a color will actually look to a human observer under real viewing conditions rather than simply specifying the color stimulus. It passes the physiological cone response through a chromatic-adaptation stage and an opponent-color stage to produce correlates of lightness, colorfulness and hue, along with chroma, saturation and brightness in the full model. Though CAM16 has since superseded it as a simpler, more robust successor, CIECAM02 remains embedded in Microsoft's Windows Color System and is still widely used for gamut mapping and cross-media color reproduction.

space.ciecam02.successor-note.t: CAM16 uses one matrix where it used two, and avoids its computational failures

space.ciecam02.use.t: Color-appearance modeling for gamut mapping and cross-media reproduction; still embedded in Windows Color System, though superseded by CAM16.

space.cineon.desc.t: Cineon — Kodak's printing-density log encoding from the early 1990s, created for the Cineon film-scanning and digital-intermediate system that first let film labs work with scanned negatives digitally instead of on an optical printer. Its 10-bit log curve maps negative density directly to code values, with reference black and white points chosen to mirror film stock's response. It has no gamut of its own — scanned imagery inherited whatever primaries the film stock and scanner implied — and it survives today mainly through the DPX file format it gave rise to.

space.cineon.use.t: Film-scanning/digital-intermediate log encoding; historical, survives mainly through the DPX file format it originated.

space.clog.desc.t: Canon Log — Canon's first cinema log gamma, introduced with the EOS C300 in 2011 to extend the dynamic range Cinema EOS cameras could capture ahead of grading. Its curve is symmetric around black, encoding a bit of below-black signal rather than clipping at zero. In this library it pairs with Canon's wide Cinema Gamut primaries, the same matrix shared with the later Canon Log 2 and Canon Log 3 curves.

space.clog.successor-note.t: Canon Log 2 held more of the newer sensors' dynamic range

space.clog.use.t: Cinema EOS camera log capture; largely superseded by Canon Log 2/3 but still supported for compatibility.

space.clog2.desc.t: Canon Log 2 — Canon's wider-latitude cinema log curve, introduced with the EOS C300 Mark II to capture more of the sensor's dynamic range than the original Canon Log. Its flatter, lower-contrast curve trades a coarser midtone step for extra stops of highlight and shadow information, intended for heavier grading later. It shares the Cinema Gamut primaries with Canon Log and Canon Log 3.

space.clog2.use.t: Cinema EOS camera log capture for maximum dynamic range; current alongside Canon Log 3.

space.clog3.desc.t: Canon Log 3 — Canon's balanced cinema log curve, added in 2016 via firmware, a cycle after the EOS C300 Mark II shipped (2015) with Canon Log 2. Rather than one log function, it blends a log shadow region, a linear midtone, and a log highlight region into a three-piece curve, aiming for close to Canon Log 2's dynamic range with gentler, easier-to-grade contrast. It shares the Cinema Gamut primaries with Canon Log and Canon Log 2, and has become Canon's most widely used cinema log curve.

space.clog3.use.t: Canon’s three-piece cinema log on Cinema Gamut; its most widely used log curve today.

space.cmy.desc.t: CMY is the subtractive color model built from cyan, magenta and yellow alone, without CMYK's separate black channel. Each channel represents how much ink is applied to absorb its complementary portion of white light, so mixing all three at full strength approximates black — though in practice impure inks produce a muddy dark brown rather than a true black, which is exactly why CMYK adds a dedicated key channel. CMY remains useful as the direct three-ink subtractive counterpart to RGB, and underlies the arithmetic CMYK is built on.

space.cmy.successor-note.t: Impure inks mix to a muddy brown, so print added a black key ink

space.cmy.use.t: Three-ink subtractive counterpart to RGB and the arithmetic base of CMYK; superseded by CMYK in print.

space.cmyk.desc.t: CMYK is the subtractive color model used throughout offset and digital printing, built from cyan, magenta and yellow inks plus a separate black channel (K, for "key"). Mixing cyan, magenta and yellow absorbs light rather than emitting it, the opposite of how RGB displays add colored light, so in principle their combination alone produces black — but real inks are impure, so a dedicated black channel keeps dark tones neutral, saves ink, and gives text and fine detail a cleaner edge. It remains the standard color model for prepress and printed output across the industry.

space.cmyk.loss-note.t: The naive device equation: many CMYK values map to one RGB (max-K convention on the way back).

space.cmyk.use.t: Subtractive four-ink model for offset / digital printing; the current prepress standard.

space.colormatch.desc.t: ColorMatch RGB – the RGB space of Radius's PressView calibrated monitors for professional graphic-arts work, shipped by Adobe as a Photoshop 5 working space. It uses P22-EBU phosphor primaries, a D50 white and gamma 1.8. Its gamut is close to sRGB's, slightly larger in the blue-greens and smaller in the red-blues, and it clips printable cyans that Adobe RGB (1998) keeps.

space.colormatch.use.t: Photoshop RGB working space modeled on Radius PressView calibrated monitors; legacy.

space.coloroid.desc.t: Coloroid — the Hungarian architectural color-order system, developed by Antal Nemcsics at the Budapest University of Technology and standardized as MSZ 7300. Grown from large-scale aesthetic experiments, it arranges hue (A), saturation (T) and luminosity (V) in steps that feel evenly spaced when composing whole environments — its home turf is architecture and urban color planning.

space.coloroid.use.t: Architectural and urban color-planning system; still used in Hungarian design practice, standardized as MSZ 7300.

space.davinci.desc.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut — Blackmagic's own wide color space and log curve, introduced in 2020 with DaVinci Resolve 17 as the default working space for Resolve's color-managed pipeline. Rather than targeting one camera, it's built as a camera-agnostic intermediate that footage from any brand can be converted into and graded consistently, similar in purpose to ACES but native to Resolve. Its DaVinci Intermediate log curve preserves highlight and shadow detail from any source camera ahead of the creative grade.

space.davinci.use.t: Camera-agnostic grading intermediate and log curve; current default working space in DaVinci Resolve's color-managed pipeline.

space.dcdm.desc.t: DCDM — the Digital Cinema Distribution Master encoding embedded in every DCP (Digital Cinema Package) shipped to theatres, standardized by SMPTE under the DCI digital cinema specification. It encodes CIE XYZ directly through a 2.6 power-law gamma rather than an RGB transfer curve, tying relative white to the DCI reference projector's calibrated brightness. It's a display-referred, deliverable-only format — content is mastered into DCDM as the last step before packaging for theatrical release.

space.dcdm.use.t: DCP deliverable encoding for theatrical projection; current mandatory format for theatrical DCP mastering (SMPTE ST 428-1).

space.dci-p3-plus.desc.t: DCI-P3+ – an expanded color gamut Canon added to the EOS C500 cinema camera's RAW development in a 2013 firmware update, wider than DCI-P3 but sharing its DCI white point (x 0.314, y 0.351). Its blue primary lies below the spectral locus (y −0.09), so part of its code range encodes no real color; Canon's Cinema Gamut, added in the same update, is wider still. Here it carries DCI-P3's pure gamma 2.6, as colour-science defines it, with the DCI white Bradford-adapted to D65 as in dci-p3.js.

space.dci-p3-plus.use.t: Expanded-gamut RAW development target of the Canon EOS C500 cinema camera; niche.

space.dci-p3.desc.t: DCI-P3 — the digital cinema standard defined in SMPTE RP 431-2 for theatrical projection and mastering. It shares its wide red-green-blue primaries with Apple's Display P3, but pairs them with the DCI theatrical white point and a pure gamma-2.6 transfer curve rather than the D65 white and sRGB-like curve used in consumer display variants. It remains the reference space for digital film production and distribution.

space.dci-p3.use.t: Reference color space for digital cinema projection and mastering; current theatrical standard, also basis of consumer Display P3.

space.dgamut.desc.t: D-Gamut – DJI's camera RGB primaries for its cinema color system, introduced in 2017 with the Zenmuse X7 and paired with the D-Log curve. DJI built it to cover Rec.709 and DCI-P3 with margin, and set each primary as nearly as possible on the line from D65 through the matching DCI-P3 primary, so hues hold when footage is gamut-mapped to P3. This is the scene-linear form, before D-Log, with highlights above 1.0.

space.dgamut.use.t: Scene-linear camera gamut beneath D-Log for DJI Zenmuse/Ronin cinema footage in VFX and grading; current.

space.din99.desc.t: DIN99 is the uniform color space of the German standard DIN 6176:2001, written by the DIN colorimetry committee (FNF/FNL 2) so that plain Euclidean distance approximates the CIE94 color difference without CIE94's weighting functions. It takes D65 CIELAB, compresses lightness logarithmically, rotates the a*b* plane by 16°, shrinks the rotated yellow-blue axis to 0.7 and compresses chroma logarithmically; a99/b99 stay in the rotated frame. DIN 6176:2018 replaced it with the refitted DIN99o and moved this formula to an appendix.

space.din99.use.t: Industrial color-tolerance measurement (coatings, plastics); legacy, superseded by DIN99o in DIN 6176:2018.

space.din99c.desc.t: DIN99c is one of three refinements of the DIN99 uniform color space published in 2002 by Cui, Luo, Rigg, Roesler and Witt, fitted to combined small color-difference data so Euclidean distance performs close to CIEDE2000. Like its sibling DIN99d it corrects the blue region by mixing a share of Z into X before the CIELAB step; unlike DIN99d it keeps the CIELAB axis orientation (no rotation) and scales the b axis by 0.94 before the logarithmic chroma compression.

space.din99c.use.t: Euclidean color-difference evaluation (blue-corrected DIN99 variant); research, not part of DIN 6176.

space.din99d.desc.t: DIN99d is a 2002 refinement of the DIN99 uniform color space by Cui, Luo, Rigg, Roesler and Witt, aimed at fixing the original formula's uneven treatment of blue hues. It adds a correction applied to the tristimulus values before the CIELAB step, along with the family's usual hue rotation and logarithmic compression, so Euclidean distance between two DIN99d points tracks perceived difference more evenly across the hue circle than DIN99 or CIELAB manage alone. Like the rest of the DIN99 family, it's used mainly for industrial color-tolerance work where a simple Euclidean metric is preferred over CIE ΔE2000.

space.din99d.use.t: Industrial color-tolerance measurement (coatings/plastics/automotive); current niche alternative to CIEDE2000.

space.din99o-lab.desc.t: DIN99o Lab is a further nonlinear remapping of CIELAB, part of the German DIN 6176 color-difference standard, built so that a simple Euclidean distance between two points approximates perceived color difference far more closely than raw CIELAB does. It compresses Lab's lightness and chroma logarithmically and applies a hue rotation, correcting CIELAB's well-known tendency to overstate differences among highly saturated colors. The DIN99 family is used mainly in industrial color-tolerance work — coatings, plastics and automotive finishes — as a lighter alternative to the more elaborate CIE ΔE2000 formula.

space.din99o-lab.use.t: Industrial color-tolerance measurement standardized in DIN 6176; current lighter alternative to CIEDE2000 in coatings/plastics/automotive QC.

space.din99o-lch.desc.t: DIN99o LCh is the cylindrical form of DIN99o Lab, the DIN 6176 color-difference space, converting its rectangular axes into chroma and hue for the same reason LCh does for ordinary CIELAB — a more direct handle for adjusting saturation and hue. It keeps DIN99o's central advantage: because the space is built so Euclidean distance already approximates perceived difference, a simple chroma or lightness difference here is a meaningful color-tolerance metric without further correction formulas.

space.din99o-lch.use.t: Direct chroma/hue tolerance adjustment; current, same industrial QC domain as DIN99o Lab.

space.dkl.desc.t: DKL — the cardinal-axis space of human color vision, proposed by Derrington, Krauskopf & Lennie in 1984 from recordings of neurons in the macaque lateral geniculate nucleus. Rather than an arbitrary opponent model, its three axes are the actual directions early visual neurons respond along: an achromatic luminance axis, an isoluminant red-green axis, and a tritan blue-yellow axis, all measured relative to an adapting white. It remains a standard framework in vision science for designing stimuli that isolate one cardinal mechanism at a time.

space.dkl.use.t: Vision-science stimulus design isolating cardinal color mechanisms; current standard framework in that research field.

space.dlog.desc.t: D-Log — DJI's log curve for its cinema-oriented cameras, including the Zenmuse X7 and Ronin 4D, designed to preserve dynamic range for grading rather than direct viewing. It pairs a linear toe near black with a log10 highlight curve, mapped to the D-Gamut primaries built for those cameras' sensors. It's distinct from D-Log M, the separate curve DJI uses on its consumer drones.

space.dlog.use.t: Log curve for DJI cinema-oriented drone/gimbal cameras; current on Zenmuse/Ronin cinema product lines.

space.donrgb4.desc.t: Don RGB 4 – a wide-gamut Photoshop working space from Don Hutcheson (HutchColor), with a D50 white and gamma 2.2, made to hold the color gamut of Ektachrome transparency film with virtually no clipping. It is distributed as an ICC profile. In Lindbloom's comparison it encloses 72.1% of the CIELAB gamut and all of the film and print color sets he tested except a sliver of the ColorChecker DC.

space.donrgb4.use.t: Wide-gamut photo and prepress working space for transparency scans; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.dsh.desc.t: CIE DSH — dominant wavelength, saturation (excitation purity) and luminance, the classical Helmholtz coordinates for CIE 1931 chromaticity. Rather than the Cartesian x, y pair, a color is located by the spectral wavelength it most resembles and how far it sits from white toward that pure spectral color — a natural way to talk about hue and saturation that predates CIELAB-style opponent spaces. Non-spectral purples, which have no single dominant wavelength, are reported as a negative complementary wavelength instead.

space.dsh.use.t: Classical dominant-wavelength / purity / luminance (Helmholtz) coordinates for CIE 1931 chromaticity.

space.dwg.desc.t: DaVinci Wide Gamut – Blackmagic Design's camera-agnostic RGB gamut, introduced in 2020 with DaVinci Resolve 17 together with the DaVinci Intermediate log curve. Blackmagic designed it to hold the vast majority of colors modern cameras capture, so footage from many sources can be stored and graded in one space before output to Rec.709 or Rec.2020. This is the scene-linear form, before the DaVinci Intermediate curve, with highlights above 1.0.

space.dwg.use.t: Scene-linear camera-agnostic working gamut beneath DaVinci Intermediate; current in DaVinci Resolve's color-managed pipeline.

space.ecirgb.desc.t: ECI RGB v2 – the RGB working space of the European Color Initiative for print-oriented image data, released in 2007 and standardized as eciRGB (2008) in ISO 22028-4. It keeps the NTSC 1953 primaries and D50 white of ECI RGB v1 (1999), but replaces v1's gamma 1.8 with the CIE L* curve: the code value is CIE lightness L* / 100, so equal code steps are equal lightness steps.

space.ecirgb.use.t: Print and prepress RGB working space; current, standardized in ISO 22028-4:2023.

space.egamut.desc.t: E-Gamut – FilmLight's wide RGB gamut for its Baselight grading systems, paired with the T-Log curve as a camera-agnostic working space that footage from many cameras is converted into for grading. All three of its primaries lie outside the spectral locus. This is the scene-linear form, before T-Log, with highlights above 1.0.

space.egamut.use.t: Scene-linear working gamut beneath T-Log; Baselight's camera-agnostic grading space.

space.ektaspace.desc.t: Ekta Space PS 5 – a working space photographer Joseph Holmes built for high-quality storage of transparency-film scans, sized to the film's gamut rather than to a display. Its blue primary lies outside the spectral locus, so a small part of its code range encodes no real color. It uses a D50 white and gamma 2.2 and is distributed as an ICC profile for Photoshop.

space.ektaspace.use.t: Working space for storing and editing transparency-film scans; niche, distributed as an ICC profile.

space.erimm.desc.t: ERIMM RGB — Kodak's Extended Reference Input Medium Metric RGB, a log-encoded, scene-referred format standardized in ISO 22028-3 as the extended-range member of the ROMM/RIMM family. It shares the wide ROMM (ProPhoto) primaries and D50 white point with ProPhoto RGB, but its logarithmic curve lets it hold a much larger range of scene exposures — well beyond diffuse white — than a linear or gamma-encoded format could, which suits archiving raw, high-dynamic-range scene data.

space.erimm.use.t: Archival log scene-referred encoding for raw HDR scene data; niche/historical, part of the Kodak ROMM/RIMM family.

space.filmicpro.desc.t: Filmic Pro 6 Log — the log curve from Filmic Pro, a third-party iOS cinema camera app that gave iPhone footage a flat, grading-ready image years before Apple Log existed natively. Its curve blends a square-root term and a natural-log term into one mixed law, built so a full-scale input maps back to a full-scale output. Like the smartphone-maker log formats that followed it, it has no published native color gamut and is treated as a curve over linear RGB.

space.filmicpro.use.t: Third-party iOS cinema-camera log capture; still available in FiLMiC Pro, overshadowed since native Apple Log arrived in 2023.

space.flog.desc.t: F-Log — Fujifilm's log curve, introduced with the X-T2 in 2016 over HDMI only and recorded in-camera from the X-H1 in 2018; firmware then brought internal F-Log to the X-T2 and other X-series and GFX cameras. It combines a linear toe in the shadows with a logarithmic highlight rolloff to extend recordable dynamic range ahead of grading. It's defined over F-Gamut, Fujifilm's color space whose primaries match ITU-R BT.2020, and remains the standard flat profile on Fujifilm bodies that lack the newer, wider-range F-Log2.

space.flog.use.t: Standard flat log profile for Fujifilm X-series/GFX video; current on bodies lacking F-Log2.

space.flog2.desc.t: F-Log2 — Fujifilm's second-generation log curve, introduced on the X-H2S to capture roughly 14 stops of dynamic range, more than the original F-Log. Its curve is shallower than F-Log's, spreading those extra stops across the code-value range at the cost of needing more careful grading. It shares the F-Gamut primaries, matching ITU-R BT.2020, with F-Log.

space.flog2.use.t: Wider-dynamic-range log profile for Fujifilm X-series/GFX video; current flagship log curve on newer bodies.

space.flog2c.desc.t: F-Log2 C — Fujifilm's F-Log2 curve recorded on F-Gamut C, a wider gamut than the BT.2020-matched F-Gamut that F-Log and F-Log2 use. Fujifilm's data sheet states the curve is identical to F-Log2, so 0%, 18% and 90% reflectance still land on 10-bit codes 95, 400 and 570; only the primaries change. F-Gamut C's red sits on ACES AP0 red, and its green and blue lie outside the spectral locus, so the gamut encloses BT.2020. Fujifilm added it to the X-H2, X-H2S and GFX100 II by firmware.

space.flog2c.use.t: F-Log2 recording on the wider F-Gamut C primaries; added to X-H2, X-H2S and GFX100 II by firmware in November 2024.

space.gplog2.desc.t: GP-Log2 — GoPro's log profile for its MISSION 1 series cameras, documented by GoPro Labs in 2026. Like Protune it is a single pure-log curve, but with log base 600 instead of 113, packing up to 14 stops into a 10-bit signal over Rec.2020 primaries. The camera meters 18% grey to code 0.5416 (about 554 of 1023) and clips about 1.8 stops above diffuse white.

space.gplog2.use.t: Log profile for GoPro MISSION 1 series cameras; graded with GoPro Labs' GP-Log2 LUT generator.

space.gray.desc.t: Gray — a single-channel relative luminance value, the Y of CIE XYZ, computed from linear-light RGB rather than gamma-encoded values. That distinction matters: true luminance (Y) measures physical light output, while the "luma" (Y′) computed from gamma-encoded RGB — common in video engineering — only approximates it. Relative luminance is the quantity behind contrast-ratio calculations such as the WCAG accessibility guidelines.

space.gray.loss-note.t: Keeps luminance only; chromaticity is discarded.

space.gray.use.t: Relative-luminance channel derived from linear RGB; current basis for WCAG contrast-ratio calculations.

space.hcg.desc.t: HCG — Hue, Chroma, Gray, a cylindrical RGB model that separates a color into its pure hue, the chroma (colorfulness) mixed into it, and the amount of gray added to dilute it. Unlike HSL or HSV, chroma here is an absolute measure of colorfulness rather than one relative to lightness or value — a natural fit for additive hue-and-gray color mixing.

space.hcg.use.t: Cylindrical RGB model (absolute chroma + gray) for colour-picker UIs; niche, mainly in JS colour libraries.

space.hcl.desc.t: HCL — a cylindrical Hue, Chroma, Luminance color space from the Chilliant rgb2hsv reference implementation. Hue and chroma behave much like other cylindrical RGB models, but luminance is computed with a gamma-weighted formula designed to track perceived brightness more closely than plain lightness or value. It is unrelated to CIE LCh, which is also sometimes called "HCL" but uses entirely different math — the two should not be confused.

space.hcl.use.t: Gamma-weighted-luminance color picking for HLSL/shader code; niche, distinct from and often confused with CIE LCh.

space.hct.desc.t: HCT — hue, chroma, tone — is Google's color space for Material Design 3, introduced in 2021 to power Android's Material You dynamic theming. It pairs the hue and chroma of CAM16, a full color-appearance model that accounts for viewing conditions, with tone: CIELAB's L* lightness, chosen because contrast and accessibility formulas already depend on it. That combination lets a design system derive a complete tonal palette from a single seed color while keeping predictable contrast between any two tones.

space.hct.use.t: Android Material You dynamic theming and tonal-palette generation; current Material Design 3 standard.

space.hcy.desc.t: HCY — Hue, Chroma, Luma, a cylindrical color model devised by Kuzma Shapran and popularized by Chilliant for real-time shader use. Unlike HSI or HSL, its Y channel is the color's actual Rec. 601 luma rather than an average or extremum of the RGB channels, and chroma is normalized against the maximum luma the current hue can carry. The result is that two colors with equal Y always read as equally bright, a property neither HSL nor HSV guarantees.

space.hcy.use.t: Luma-consistent hue model for real-time shader color grading; niche, used in HLSL/GLSL graphics code.

space.hdr-cie-lab.desc.t: hdr-CIELAB — Fairchild & Wyble's 2010/2011 extension of CIELAB to high-dynamic-range imagery. CIELAB's cube-root lightness response was fit to ordinary display luminance and breaks down across HDR's wider range, so hdr-CIELAB substitutes a Michaelis-Menten response whose exponent adapts to scene luminance, in the spirit of human visual adaptation. It keeps CIELAB's familiar L*, a* and b* lightness and red-green/yellow-blue structure while extending it to HDR content.

space.hdr-cie-lab.successor-note.t: HDR image-difference work moved to HDR-native spaces such as ICtCp and Jzazbz

space.hdr-cie-lab.use.t: HDR-adapted CIELAB for wide-luminance-range image-difference work; academic, superseded in practice by ICtCp/Jzazbz.

space.hdr-ipt.desc.t: hdr-IPT — Fairchild & Wyble's 2010/2011 extension of IPT to high-dynamic-range imagery. IPT's fixed power-law lightness response only holds over a narrow luminance range, so hdr-IPT replaces it with a Michaelis-Menten response whose exponent adapts to the scene's own luminance, echoing how the eye itself adapts. It keeps IPT's I/P/T lightness, red-green and yellow-blue structure while extending its hue-linear behavior across HDR's much larger dynamic range.

space.hdr-ipt.use.t: HDR-adapted IPT for hue-linear appearance modeling across wide luminance range; academic, not industrially deployed.

space.hellwig2022.desc.t: The Hellwig-Fairchild model, published in 2022, is the CIE-recommended refinement of CAM16 and the mathematical basis of CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022). It keeps CAM16's chromatic-adaptation transform, opponent-color dimensions, and lightness correlate largely intact, but revises the achromatic response and brightness equations for more consistent behavior across the model's full range. Like CAM16 it reports lightness, colorfulness, and hue as its core correlates — a close drop-in successor wherever a CIE-endorsed appearance model is called for.

space.hellwig2022.use.t: CIE-recommended color-appearance model succeeding CAM16; current mathematical basis of CIECAM16 (CIE 248:2022).

space.helmgen.desc.t: HelmGen is the generation space (GenSpace) of Helmlab, published by Görkem Yıldız in 2026 for UI design systems. It keeps Oklab's shape (cone-like LMS, a compressive transfer, an opponent matrix) but swaps the cube root for a depressed cubic y³ + αy = x, whose finite slope at zero removes the dark-end cusp singularities, then adds a mild chroma power, a piecewise lightness correction and a lightness-gated hue twist in the blues that keeps a blue-to-white gradient sky blue instead of lavender. Fit to gradient benchmarks rather than color-difference data; its sibling MetricSpace takes that role.

space.helmgen.use.t: Gradients, palettes and color-mix in design systems; new, shipped in Color.js 0.7.

space.helmgenlch.desc.t: HelmGen LCh is the cylindrical form of Helmlab's 2026 generation space: lightness, chroma and hue over HelmGen's opponent plane, the form for hue-led gradients, palette ramps and color-mix in design systems.

space.helmgenlch.use.t: Hue-led palettes and gradients in design systems; new, shipped in Color.js 0.7.

space.hpluv.desc.t: HPLuv is the pastel counterpart to HSLuv, from the same project by Alexei Boronine. Instead of fitting saturation to the sRGB gamut boundary at each individual hue, it uses the single largest circle that fits inside the gamut at a given lightness, so every hue stays reachable across the full saturation range — at the cost of never reaching fully vivid colors, since S=100 only means as saturated as the least colorful hue at that lightness allows. Lightness and hue pass through unchanged from LCHuv, just as in HSLuv; only the chroma mapping differs.

space.hpluv.use.t: Guaranteed-in-gamut pastel companion to HSLuv for palette tools; current, maintained alongside HSLuv.

space.hsi.desc.t: HSI — Hue, Saturation, Intensity, a cylindrical color model popular in image processing and computer vision. Intensity is simply the average of the red, green and blue channels, which decouples brightness from color information more cleanly than HSV or HSL for tasks like segmentation and feature extraction, at the cost of a more involved saturation calculation than its cousins.

space.hsi.use.t: Image-processing / computer-vision hue-saturation-intensity model; still used in segmentation and remote sensing.

space.hsl.desc.t: HSL — Hue, Saturation, Lightness, a cylindrical remapping of RGB first described by George Joblove and Donald Greenberg in 1978, beside Alvy Ray Smith's HSV. Hue is the angle around a color wheel, saturation measures colorfulness relative to gray at that lightness, and lightness runs from black through the pure hue up to white. It offers a far more intuitive way to pick and adjust colors than raw RGB, and underlies the `hsl()` notation in CSS and countless color-picker interfaces.

space.hsl.use.t: Intuitive hue/saturation/lightness color picking; current, standardized as CSS's hsl().

space.hsluv.desc.t: HSLuv is Alexei Boronine's human-friendly cylindrical form of CIELUV, built to fix a longstanding frustration with HSL: at full saturation, different hues reach wildly different actual vividness, so pure yellow at S=100 looks nothing like pure blue at S=100. HSLuv rescales chroma per hue and lightness so that S=100 always lands exactly on the sRGB gamut boundary, giving a saturation slider that behaves consistently across every hue. Lightness and hue pass through unchanged from LCHuv, and the result is popular in design tools and palette generators that want HSL's familiar interface without its uneven color behavior.

space.hsluv.use.t: Perceptually even saturation across hues for design/palette tools; current, actively maintained (renamed from HUSL in 2018).

space.hsm.desc.t: HSM — Hue, Saturation, Mixture, developed by Bianconi et al. (2009) for robust skin-color detection in image processing. Mixture is a luminance-weighted average of the red, green and blue channels standing in for brightness, while saturation measures how far a color sits from that gray mixture relative to the farthest a color at the same mixture level can reach, keeping saturation properly bounded across the whole range of mixture values.

space.hsm.use.t: Skin-color detection in image processing; academic, niche.

space.hsp.desc.t: HSP — Hue, Saturation, Perceived brightness, a cylindrical color model designed to fix a known flaw in HSL and HSV, where lightness and value don't match how bright colors actually look to the human eye. Perceived brightness is instead computed from a weighted mix of the red, green and blue channels that reflects the eye's differing sensitivity to each, so two colors with the same P value look equally bright regardless of hue.

space.hsp.use.t: Perceived-brightness color picker alternative to HSL/HSV; niche hobbyist and creative-coding use.

space.hsv.desc.t: HSV — Hue, Saturation, Value (also called HSB, for Brightness), another cylindrical remapping of RGB from Alvy Ray Smith's 1978 paper. It shares HSL's hue angle but replaces lightness with value, the brightness of the most intense color channel, so pure hues stay fully saturated across the whole brightness range instead of washing out toward white. It is the model behind most color-picker "wheel plus square" interfaces.

space.hsv.use.t: Hue/saturation/value color picking with pure hues at full brightness; current, the standard 'wheel plus square' picker model.

space.hunt.desc.t: Hunt — Robert Hunt's colour appearance model (1982-1995), the most ambitious of the classical CAMs: developed over decades at Kodak, it models cone AND rod responses, luminance-level adaptation, surround induction, and predicts the full set of appearance correlates for related and unrelated colours from dim starlight to bright daylight. Its complexity is legendary — and directly ancestral: CIECAM97s and CIECAM02 are, in Fairchild's phrase, Hunt models simplified for practice.

space.hunt.use.t: Historical flagship appearance model (Kodak); the direct ancestor of CIECAM97s/CIECAM02; kept for study.

space.hunter-rdab.desc.t: Hunter Rd,a,b is Richard Hunter's earliest opponent-color scale, developed in 1943 for illuminant C so that early analog tristimulus colorimeters could report a color as reflectance plus red-green and yellow-blue values. Rd is the CIE Y value itself; a and b are linear differences of normalized X, Y, Z, scaled by a factor f(Y) that grows toward black to keep the dark end of the chromatic scales from collapsing. It preceded Hunter L,a,b (1958, see labh) and survives in a few industries, notably as a brightness reading for neutral limestone-based powders.

space.hunter-rdab.use.t: Single-number brightness/reflectance of neutral limestone-based powders; legacy, rarely used today.

space.hwb.desc.t: HWB — Hue, Whiteness, Blackness, devised by Alvy Ray Smith in 1996 as an even more intuitive alternative to HSV for humans mixing colors by hand. Instead of saturation and value, it describes a color as a pure hue diluted with some amount of white and some amount of black, mirroring how painters think about tinting and shading a pigment. It is standardized in CSS Color 4 as the `hwb()` notation.

space.hwb.use.t: Intuitive tint/shade color picking; current, standardized as CSS Color 4's hwb().

space.iapbp.desc.t: IaPbP is a uniform color space for HDR and wide-gamut images published by Huang et al. in 2024. It keeps IPT's layout (cone matrix, per-cone nonlinearity, opponent matrix) but makes both matrices 4×4 projective transforms in homogeneous coordinates and replaces the power law with SA-PQ, a PQ-shaped curve fitted to a surround-aware contrast sensitivity function for a 500 lx room. The parameters were optimized jointly for uniformity, hue linearity and low crosstalk between lightness and chroma.

space.iapbp.use.t: Uniform opponent space for HDR/WCG image processing (tone mapping, color difference); research, no reference implementation.

space.icacb.desc.t: ICaCb — an HDR opponent space designed by Fröhlich in 2017, built in the same mold as ICtCp but re-optimized for just-noticeable-difference uniformity and straighter hue lines. XYZ passes through a dedicated cone matrix and the PQ (ST 2084) non-linearity before the opponent mix, giving I as intensity and Ca/Cb as red-green and yellow-blue chroma.

space.icacb.use.t: HDR/wide-gamut opponent space re-optimized for JND uniformity versus ICtCp; research use, not broadly adopted industrially.

space.ictcp-hlg.desc.t: ICtCp with the HLG transfer is the second ICtCp variant in ITU-R BT.2100: the same Rec. 2020 to LMS cone matrix as PQ ICtCp, but each cone signal is coded with the Hybrid Log-Gamma OETF on scene light, and the Ct and Cp rows are the PQ rows scaled by about 0.55 and 0.53. It gives HLG chains ICtCp's constant-intensity chroma as an alternative to Y′C′bC′r.

space.ictcp-hlg.use.t: Constant-intensity opponent coding for HLG HDR; standardized, but BT.2100 keeps NCL Y′C′bC′r as the default and reserves ICtCp for exchange by mutual agreement.

space.ictcp.desc.t: ICtCp — Dolby's HDR opponent space, standardized in ITU-R BT.2100 for HDR television. Intensity rides the PQ curve while Ct and Cp carry blue-yellow and red-green chroma, keeping hue stable under big luminance changes — the space HDR colorists grade in and the basis of the ΔE-ITP difference metric.

space.ictcp.use.t: HDR television color grading and the dE-ITP difference metric; current ITU-R BT.2100 standard for HDR broadcast/streaming.

space.igpgtg.desc.t: IgPgTg is a color space proposed by Hensley and Fairchild in 2020 as a lighter-weight alternative to CAM16-UCS for hue-uniform color-difference work. Structurally it follows IPT, deriving a lightness signal from LMS cone responses and pairing it with two opponent channels — named Ig, Pg and Tg for intensity, protan and tritan, after the color-vision deficiencies their axes roughly align with. The authors report hue uniformity competitive with CAM16-UCS at a fraction of the computational cost.

space.igpgtg.use.t: Lightweight hue-uniform alternative to CAM16-UCS for color-difference work; academic, not widely deployed.

space.ihls.desc.t: IHLS, Improved HLS, is a 3D-polar remapping of RGB introduced by Allan Hanbury in 2003, building on a 2002 technical report with Jean Serra. Hue is the exact angle in the chromatic plane, saturation is max(R,G,B) − min(R,G,B) and brightness is Rec. 709 weighted luma. Saturation therefore stays small for every near-gray and does not depend on brightness, whereas HLS divides by lightness and can call a near-black color fully saturated. It was designed for image analysis: hue statistics, saturation-weighted hue histograms and color morphology.

space.ihls.use.t: Hue/saturation features for image analysis and color morphology; research niche.

space.ilog.desc.t: Insta360 I-Log — Insta360's log profile, here in the 10-bit container curve of its June 2026 white paper (revision 2026.05.20). A log10 curve rises from a short linear toe and holds scene reflectance from black to 2200%, about 7 stops over middle grey, on BT.2020 primaries with a D65 white. 0% lands at 0.0906 (10-bit code 93) and 18% grey at 0.4220 (code 432). The paper's version history shows the curve has changed: an initial version in 2024, a new transfer function for the 10-bit container in July 2025, and a bug fix before the final release.

space.ilog.use.t: Log profile for Insta360's 10-bit I-Log cameras (X6, Luna Ultra); graded with Insta360's official I-Log LUTs.
